sources.title: Trump, Starmer discuss reopening Hormuz Strait as Iran blockade disrupts shipping
sources.snippet: KANANASKIS, ALBERTA - JUNE 16: U.S. President Donald Trump and British Prime Minister Keir Starmer walk together after singing a trade deal as they leave a bilateral meeting during the G7 Leaders' Summit on June 16, 2025 in Kananaskis, Alberta. Canada is hosting this year's meeting of the world's seven largest economies./AFP (Photo by CHIP SOMODEVILLA / GETTY IMAGES NORTH AMERICA / Getty Images via AFP) US President Donald Trump and British Prime Minister Keir Starmer spoke Sunday about the 'importance' of reopening the Strait of Hormuz, currently blocked by Iran, the UK leader's office said. 'The leaders discussed the ongoing situation in the Middle East and the importance of reopening the Strait of Hormuz to end the disruption to global shipping, which is driving up costs worldwide,' a Downing Street spokeswoman said in a statement. On Saturday, Trump urged other countries such as China, France, Japan, South Korea and Britain to send warships to help the United States secure the strait. Iran's military is effectively blocking the crucial waterway in retaliation for US-Israeli strikes, aiming to damage the world economy and pressure Washington as oil prices soar. Starmer also 'expressed his condolences for the American service personnel who have lost their lives during the conflict', the statement said. AFP

sources.title: Pete Hegseth warns Iran is jeopardizing safe oil shipping via Strait of Hormuz
sources.snippet: Tensions around the Strait of Hormuz are rising again as the Pentagon accuses Iran of threatening one of the world’s most critical oil routes. U.S. War Secretary Pete Hegseth claimed the waterway remains technically open but warned that Iranian attacks on shipping are the only thing stopping vessels from passing safely. America’s top military leadership doubled down during a Pentagon briefing, placing direct blame on Tehran for the disruption to global trade. With nearly a fifth of the world’s oil moving through Hormuz, the latest claims are fueling fears of a dangerous escalation in the Gulf.

sources.title: 'Vital to open Strait of Hormuz': Japan releases emergency oil reserves amid Israel-Iran conflict
sources.snippet: Tokyo: Japan has commenced the release of oil from its private-sector reserves to bolster supply stability as the ongoing conflict with Iran continues to impede maritime traffic in the Middle East, NHK reported. According to the broadcaster, the volume of fuel currently being released corresponds to "15 days of consumption." Industry data indicates that "oil-related companies in Japan hold reserves equivalent to 70 days." In addition to these private stocks, the Japanese government maintains an independent emergency reserve and is "expected to release one month of supply later in March." Currently, Japan's total emergency petroleum reserves account for 254 days of national demand, composed of national stockpiles, private sector reserves, and joint stockpiles with producing nations. This move follows a broader international effort by the International Energy Agency (IEA), which announced that nations across Asia Oceania will release 108.6 million barrels of oil "immediately." IEA Executive Director Fatih Birol confirmed that "unprecedented additional volumes of oil" are being introduced to the global market to mitigate the crisis. However, Birol cautioned that while the release will assist supply, "opening the Strait of Hormuz is vital for a return to stable flows" as the maritime route remains a critical bottleneck for global energy security. Amidst these energy concerns, diplomatic efforts to secure the waterway have intensified. Japanese Defence Minister Shinjiro Koizumi held discussions with US Secretary of War Pete Hegseth, reaffirming Tokyo's stance on the necessity of preserving peace and stability within the Strait of Hormuz. sources.title: Faced with Iran's threat to shipping, the G7 hopes to escort tankers and cargo ships through the Strait of Hormuz with warships
sources.snippet: G7 countries will send warships to accompany tankers and cargo ships passing through the Strait of Hormuz. French President Emmanuel Macron said after a video conference on the economic consequences of the war in Iran, chaired by G7 heads of state and government, that to ensure the smooth progress of such escorts, it was necessary to coordinate the navies of several countries and preliminary work in previous weeks. 'This condition has not yet been met. The Channel is a war zone, but the work must be organized. That is what we are proposing, working with shipping companies, transport companies and insurance companies at the same time.' The G7 countries include Germany, the United States, Japan, Canada, the United Kingdom, France and Italy. Iran threatened to sink all ships passing through the strait after Israel and the United States attacked the Iranian regime. The United States has sunk 28 Iranian minelayers and almost all of its naval warships. France has also deployed three large warships to the region, and Italy, Britain and the Netherlands have also sent naval vessels to the Mediterranean. Naval forces have protected merchant ships in the Red Sea since 2024. There, Houthi militias hostile to Israel and backed by the Iranian regime threaten shipping in the region. Experts believe that with the gathering of G7 warships in the Strait of Hormuz, a "mass fight" against the Iranian regime has in fact formed, which is of course a great thing for world shipping, especially since the three East Asian countries are heavily dependent on the oil shipped from the Strait of Hormuz and would not have increased if they were not dependent on oil prices.
